title: ⭐⭐ Revision: owners, tenses and a road at night

questions.prompt: You have one brother, and his car has stopped working. Which sentence is correct English?

options.text: My brothers car broke down on the motorway.
My brothers's car broke down on the motorway.
My brother car's broke down on the motorway.
My brother's car broke down on the motorway.

questions.explanation: "My brother's car broke down on the motorway." is correct: one owner, so the apostrophe and the s go on the owner, immediately before what he owns. "My brothers car broke down on the motorway." drops the apostrophe and turns the owner into a plural. "My brother car's broke down on the motorway." marks the thing owned instead of the owner, and "My brothers's car broke down on the motorway." builds a plural you do not have here.

questions.prompt: Complete this line from a driver's notebook: "Her worst fear was ___ on that empty road at night."

options.text: a journey
a rear-view mirror
a breakdown
a headlight

questions.explanation: "a breakdown" is the word: it names the moment a car stops working, and being left with a dead engine on an empty road at night is a real fear. "a journey" is only the trip itself, which she has chosen to make. "a headlight" is one of the lamps at the front, and "a rear-view mirror" is the mirror showing what follows her; neither of those two objects is frightening on its own.

questions.prompt: Read this sentence from the story: "The hairs on my neck stood up." What is the infinitive of the irregular verb it contains?

options.text: to stand
to stay
to stick
to stood

questions.explanation: "to stand" is the infinitive: stood is its simple past, and the past participle is stood as well. "to stood" repeats the past form after to, which no infinitive ever does. "to stay" and "to stick" are two other verbs whose sound is close, but neither of them has stood among its forms: they give stayed and stuck.

questions.prompt: A classmate has just told you something and you did not follow it at all. Which sentence do you use?

options.text: Is this what you wanted?
What a nice view!
What about another cup of tea?
What do you mean exactly?

questions.explanation: "What do you mean exactly?" asks for a clarification: you are not asking for a new fact, you are asking your classmate to say the same thing again in clearer words. "What about another cup of tea?" offers an idea, "Is this what you wanted?" checks whether somebody is satisfied, and "What a nice view!" only shows admiration.

questions.prompt: The other car overtook her, braked, and then stayed behind her again however slowly she drove. Why did that frighten the narrator?

options.text: Because her own car had broken down on the way.
Because the driver had switched off his headlights.
Because the driver seemed to be following her on purpose.
Because the road was full of lorries and buses at that hour.

questions.explanation: "Because the driver seemed to be following her on purpose." is the reason: a car that overtakes has no reason to fall back, and one that copies her speed is matching her, not travelling its own way. "Because the driver had switched off his headlights." invents a detail, since she watches those lamps in her mirror all along. "Because the road was full of lorries and buses at that hour." contradicts the empty road, and "Because her own car had broken down on the way." would have stopped the story long before.

questions.prompt: Who tells this story, and what does the text let you know about her?

options.text: A nurse who works at the rehabilitation centre.
A woman whose husband is being treated after an illness.
A young girl who has just passed her driving test.
A journalist who followed a car for a newspaper.

questions.explanation: "A woman whose husband is being treated after an illness." is the narrator: she says my husband Donald, she leaves him at the centre, and she has a married son, so she is not a young woman. "A young girl who has just passed her driving test." cannot have a son old enough to be married. "A journalist who followed a car for a newspaper." makes her the follower instead of the followed, and "A nurse who works at the rehabilitation centre." turns a visitor into a member of the staff.
